articles.title: Jason Snell’s HomeView Review
articles.summary:
Jason Snell:
The hardware is solid and coherent, the screen a pleasure to touch
and tilt. In terms of software, though, the HomeView feels like a
peculiar amalgam of numerous other Apple products. Its main
interface makes it look a bit like an overgrown Apple Watch,
complete with customizable “faces” that sometimes resemble actual
Apple Watch faces and other times resemble the iPhone’s StandBy
mode. Its apps sometimes feel like they’ve escaped from the iPhone
or iPad, but at other times they feel more like they’re right off
of an Apple TV. And still other “apps” resemble what you might see
in your car, since Apple is also using CarPlay to project
interfaces from apps running on your iPhone.
Given the fact that this product’s tech stack feels like it
was created in a blender, it’s remarkable that it holds
together as well as it does — but there are still places
where the seams show.
I’ve been testing a review unit HomeView for a bit over a week, but haven’t had much time to devote to it. So in a lot of ways my HomeView experience thus far has been much more like that of a casual user than an expert. I plugged it in, set it up, got my wife and son to do what they needed to do to become recognized fellow-family-member users, and then we all collectively have had a week of “Well, now what?”
What Snell writes above succinctly and sharply describes my take: the hardware is top-notch but the software is like bits of iOS, WatchOS, tvOS, and CarPlay cut up and assembled into a ransom letter. The software lacks cohesion and vision and polish. If you open a web page you can select text, with the iOS touch interface, but there is nothing you can do with a text selection. You can’t copy it or share it. So why can you even make a selection? That’s the least of HomeView’s software problems, but perhaps most emblematic of its “created in a blender” state.
 ★

articles.title: This Week in Package Management: 14 November 2026
articles.summary:
This week’s package management news, gathered from the package manager OPML feed collection, my posts and boosts on Mastodon, and anything people sent me. Version control and forge news is in the Wednesday This Week in Source Control roundup.
Security
Composer 2.11.2 fixes seven security bugs, two of them reachable through a crafted composer.lock or vendor/composer/installed.json. Those are arbitrary command execution through the prevent_url_access_callable transport option (GHSA-jhfp-4ppm-crmm) and inline repository HTTP credentials sent to dist mirrors on other hosts (GHSA-x82q-x274-r6pq).
A malicious zip could also write outside the package directory through symlinked entries when extraction fell back from unzip to ZipArchive (GHSA-w6hj-6587-3jh5). Composer 2.2.32 backports the zip and credential fixes to the LTS branch. 2.11.2 also adds an exclude-branches option for VCS repositories and aborts downloads that stall for 30 seconds.
Podman 6.2.0 and 5.8.10 fix three CVEs, one of which let untrusted image labels make podman auto-update restart the wrong systemd units (GHSA-55rm-rwr7-q2wr). The other two are a digest and signature validation bypass for malicious images (GHSA-pggw-qqjf-6cxw) and a bypass of the socket deny rule in the default seccomp profile. 6.2.0 also adds podman push --platform, which pushes one platform’s manifest instead of the whole list.
pnpm 11.28.12 makes a ${VAR} placeholder in a registry URL in pnpm-workspace.yaml or the project .npmrc fail the command. pnpm does not expand environment variables in those files, and earlier versions skipped such a URL and resolved packages from another registry, such as npmjs.org.
From 8 December, GitHub will turn off Dependabot alerts on most repositories whose last activity is more than a year old. Activity means a push to any branch or tag, creating the repository, or turning alerts on. Existing alerts are archived, and any push restores them and restarts the one-year period. Repositories under an enforced security configuration that enables Dependabot alerts are exempt.
Releases
Rust 1.100.0 stabilises Cargo’s min-publish-age: setting global-min-publish-age = "3 days" under [registry] in .cargo/config.toml makes the resolver skip versions published more recently than that, and cargo update lists what it held back. Versions missing a pubtime in the index are always eligible, and cargo install resolves without the setting.
Cargo also now warns about unused dependencies, as part of a new linting system configured through the [lints.cargo] table. The warning appears only when every build target that could use the dependency is built, and it skips dev-dependencies.
pnpm 12.19.0 adds pnpm fund and an experimental lockfile.format: v13 setting. The new format writes pnpm-lock.yaml in a JSON-like syntax that is still valid YAML, with one entry per package version, so updating a peer dependency changes only the lines that record its version. 12.21.0 lets pnpm store add prepare tarball and git dependencies for offline installs.
vlt 1.7.0 adds vlt deploy and vlt update <pkg> and locks git dependencies to a commit, and 1.8.0 installs from vlt’s public npm mirror with no setup and resolves unprefixed dependencies from the project’s own registry configuration.
mise 2026.11.4 (now 2026.11.8) accepts zip:: archives over HTTP or HTTPS for config and task includes. The contents behind the URL can change between fetches, and paranoid mode rejects zip config includes. From 2026.11.6, [bootstrap.packages] keys without a manager: prefix install through the first available system package manager, and the npm backend can install from an HTTPS tarball URL.
uv 0.13.8 extends the wheel variants preview to local paths, direct URLs and Git repositories, and detects x86-64 microarchitecture levels when selecting a variant. Plaintext credential files on Unix are now restricted to owner-only permissions.
Homebrew 7.0.13 adds a pin: true Brewfile option and prefetches bottle attestations in bulk. All official casks now require a zap stanza.
Harbor 2.16.0 replaces Redis with Valkey as the cache backend and ships images for arm64 as well as amd64. Proxy cache projects can now pass OCI referrers API requests to the upstream registry and merge the results with local ones.
Renovate 44.228.0 to 44.239.1 adds a gemspec manager that updates dependency constraints in *.gemspec files, and the swift manager now updates .package(id:) dependencies from Swift package registries. With the experimental minimumReleaseAgePackageManagerSync option, Renovate reads the release age configured for pnpm, Yarn, Cargo and Poetry and runs each tool with the longer of that and its own minimumReleaseAge, and npm’s min-release-age in .npmrc is read too. renovate-config-validator --migrate now writes out a migrated config file for configs that use old option names.
Also out:
Gradle 9.9.1
Gradle 8.14.7
Maven 3.10.1
pixi 0.84.2
pnpr 0.1.0-alpha.20
Pkg.jl 1.13.4
Nix 2.35.6
DNF5 5.4.8.0
Go 1.27.4
Go 1.26.11
Helm 4.3.2
Terraform 1.17.2
Dependabot Core 0.404.0
NuGet Client 8.2.0.11
PSResourceGet 1.3.1
Harbor 2.15.5
Docker Engine 29.10.0-rc.2
Articles
Artifact integrity for Packagist and Composer (Packagist blog) announces Alpha-Omega funding for Packagist.org to store package artifacts itself. Today it hosts only metadata, and more than 99% of versions point at a zip that GitHub generates on demand from the git repository. Those archives differ between GitHub servers and can change over time, so most packages have an empty checksum field. The funded work has five phases:
Permanent artifact storage, with checksums in the package metadata and the transparency log
A Sigstore signature and build provenance attestation for every stored artifact, verified by Composer
API tokens limited to specific packages and permissions, with expiry and automatic revocation when leaked
Trusted Publishing from CI workflows through OIDC
Artifact uploads and a composer publish command, with staged releases approved by hardware key
Uploads and Trusted Publishing will ship only together with mandatory signing and attestations. Stored artifacts also make it possible to publish several packages from one repository, which today requires splitting a monorepo into read-only mirrors.
Lock your GitHub Actions (Hugo van Kemenade) shows how to adopt GitHub’s workflow lockfiles. The gh actions-lock extension rewrites SHA-pinned uses: lines back to version tags and records each tag’s commit, owner ID and repository ID in .github/workflows/actions.lock. Renovate and Dependabot both update the lockfile, and a CI job running gh actions-lock --verify fails when the lockfile is out of sync with the workflows.
Farid Zakaria has two posts on running builds inside Rewind, the deterministic virtual machine he is building. Making profile-guided optimization reproducible starts from Nixpkgs disabling profile-guided builds of Python and GCC because the training run varies between builds. What if every Nix build were bit-reproducible? wraps derivations in the VM so that content-addressed builds produce the same store path on every machine, with the VM version as a build input.
Bringing v1 recipes to conda-build (conda blog) explains how conda-build now builds recipe.yaml recipes by dispatching to the Python bindings for the rattler-build crates. The existing build, render and debug subcommands handle both formats, and options unsupported on the v1 path raise an error. Maintainers with large collections of meta.yaml recipes can move them to the v1 format and keep their existing conda-build pipelines.
Swift’s November news digest opens with a reminder from Dave Verwer that CocoaPods stops accepting new pods and pod versions on 2 December 2026. Current pods and versions will still be served, read-only, so the change does not immediately break builds. Verwer also writes that he is now part of a team at Apple working on a public, cross-platform package registry for Swift.
python-sbom (Bernát Gábor) is a build plugin that writes a CycloneDX 1.6 SBOM into every wheel under .dist-info/sboms/, the directory defined for SBOMs in the installed packages specification. It has plugins for hatchling, pdm-backend and setuptools and a wrapper backend for other build backends. The SBOM records the source commit, the interpreter, the build tools and any wheels the project bundles as data files.
Alpha-Omega published a case study of the PHP2Shell response. Volker Dusch, the PHP Foundation’s Security Engineer in Residence, coordinated with researchers, Linux distributions and WAF vendors while the core engineers wrote the fixes. PHP’s security team received more than 200 reports in the week after disclosure, many of them duplicates, and built TAMIS, which compares incoming reports against existing ones several times a day.
Reproducible Builds in October 2026 reports that GNU tar embeds its process ID in the member path when it writes a sparse file to a PAX archive, so identical inputs produce a different archive on each run. Robin Candau and Bernhard M. Wiedemann have also revived a shared repository of reproducibility patches, which currently holds patches from openSUSE and Arch Linux.
Elsewhere
I am tired (Kushal Das) describes finding more than 90 vulnerabilities since July in open source projects, many of them written or used by Sunet, with LLM help and 16-hour days. Das writes that most maintainers and defenders of that infrastructure have neither the model access nor the hardware to do the same.
Dawn Foster published the video and slides of her Community Over Code talk, Good Governance for Sustainable Open Source Projects, with links to her five-part series on the same topics.
Anil Madhavapeddy is using brief, which I wrote, to detect the languages and toolchains in a repository for automatic CI in his Tangled spindle.
An Empirical Study of Observability Limits in Advanced Software Supply Chain Attacks (Zhuoran Tan et al., CCS) introduces SynthChain, a runtime telemetry dataset built from seven attack scenarios across PyPI, npm and C++ supply chains. The best single telemetry source recovers fewer than 40% of the expected attack steps. Combining two complementary sources improves reconstruction by roughly 1.6 times.
git-pkgs
I tagged 7 repos this week:
git-pkgs v0.22.0
attestation v0.2.0
brief v0.16.0
manifests v0.14.0
pin v0.2.2
registries v0.13.2
signals v0.2.0
Send links for next week to @andrewnez@mastodon.social.

articles.title: Patrick McGee on Johny Srouji and Nvidia
articles.summary:
Patrick McGee (author of Apple in China; my guest on The Talk Show last May), writing on X in response to Semafor’s reporting that Nvidia is “considering” Johny Srouji:
Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji would be an incredible choice to
lead @nvidia — and I believe he’d accept it.
He’s hit the ceiling at Apple and won’t ever be CEO; obviously
competent; ambitious as hell; has long wanted chip designs to
dictate Apple product launches/timelines.
I wrote about this a few days ago, that my money is on Srouji having no interest in the Nvidia job. It’s true that Srouji will almost certainly never be CEO at Apple. But it’s wrong to assume that Srouji would consider CEO of Nvidia to be an upgrade from CHO at Apple. There’s no way Eddy Cue, Craig Federighi, or Greg Joswiak would leave Apple to be CEO at another company. Most of Apple’s leadership genuinely bleeds six colors. There’s a certain approach to product that drives them, motivates them, and literally only Apple does that type of work. Tim Cook surely turned down numerous CEO offers to leave Apple while he served as COO under Steve Jobs, and he’s always been clear that he hoped Jobs would stay a few steps ahead of his cancer and could remain at Apple until, well, probably around now. (Jobs would be 71.)
I’ve never met Srouji and don’t have a read on him like I do other leaders at Apple. But I do have a read on Ternus and Cook. I’ll stick with my bet from earlier in the week:
Another scenario is that Srouji meant what he said, loves his job
at Apple, and truly is John Ternus’s trusted and trustworthy
hardware lieutenant. In this case, Nvidia’s board leaking that
they’re considering Srouji to replace Huang is like someone in
hell saying they’re considering ordering some ice water.
Aside from Srouji’s loyalty to Apple (and to the Apple Silicon chip architecture that’s been his life’s work), there’s also the question of whether he’d take the gig at Nvidia in particular, even if he is open to leaving Apple. Jensen Huang has left the company with a $4 trillion market cap, yes, but it was $5 trillion just a week ago. It now seems 20 percent of Nvidia’s sales in the AI era have been in violation of U.S. national security export controls to China. The company has no internal leadership hierarchy. And Huang placed bets that have leveraged the company’s future on OpenAI and the overall data center mania not being a bubble. Srouji has been a senior leader at the one tech company that conspicuously avoided those bets entirely.
 ★

articles.title: Of Course People Hate Data Centres
articles.summary:
The breakout issue of 2026 has undoubtedly been data centres, more precisely opposition to data centres. People despise them. In the US midterms, only a single ballot measure (out of 44) on data centres resulted in a favourable outcome for the developers. In exit polls conducted by CBS News, 76% of respondents oppose construction of data centres in their community – and it’s not just Democrats (87% oppose): opposition among Republicans (62% oppose) and independents (78% oppose) is high too. Simultaneously, views on AI are bleak, with 57% of respondents saying it will do more to hurt humanity than to help; only 24% say it will help more. In Europe, 92 protests against data centres are being organised in November alone. Those in tech have been caught off guard, and many don’t seem to understand this strong opposition. I think it’s obvious.
I’m sure there’s always been opposition to heavy industry. No one wants to live next to a chemical plant. However, this feels different. We’ve been building data centres without major issues for nearly a century. What’s different this time?
Perhaps it’s scale. Cleanview, a market intelligence company, puts the total number of data centres operating or being constructed in the US at 1,835. Ten years ago the figure was a fifth of that (352). In 2026 alone, the number has increased by ~60%, from 1,134 the year before. The data centres being built are also bigger than ever, both when measured in square metres and power consumption.
However, more than anything, I think people hate AI and its proponents. It doesn’t help that the companies and people who are central to the development of AI spent the 2010s cultivating a bad reputation as “big tech”. Neither do their public statements of impending doom due to runaway RSI (Recursive Self-Improvement) or massive white-collar job displacement causing a permanent underclass. These proponents will counter that AI will usher in an era of unprecedented civilisational progress. It will solve our biggest problems: disease, climate change, and poverty, with only a slight risk of total extinction.
In his book Life 3.0, Max Tegmark explores potential scenarios if we achieve AGI (Artificial General Intelligence). One of these, Egalitarian Utopia, describes a world in which machines have made work redundant, private property has been abolished, and everything is free because the cost of production has collapsed. Humans spend their time on leisure, art, or whatever else they fancy, all their needs taken care of. By contrast, the 2013 film Elysium describes a world in which the rich and powerful live a life in orbit similar to Tegmark’s scenario, but on Earth the majority eke out a meagre, gruesome existence.
Tegmark’s scenario certainly sounds appealing, and if your p(doom) is 0%, then full speed ahead at nearly any cost seems a sound conclusion. Of course, most people don’t put p(doom) at 0% – Tegmark, for example, puts it at 90%. Regardless, with wealth inequality on the rise and the richest few controlling more resources (including the frontier AI labs) than ever, most people probably view the Elysium outcome, or something like it, as far more probable.
Even among tech enthusiasts, some of whom are making significant use of AI, there’s a great deal of animosity towards the frontier labs and their executives. Sam Altman’s recent comment about it being “quite terrible” for some of the world’s limited supply of RAM to be in the hands of private individuals was not appreciated in those circles. If I were in charge of marketing at OpenAI, I would push for a ban on Altman making public statements. The data centre build-out has pushed the price and availability of RAM and GPUs out of reach for enthusiasts. In recent months, many old games have been resurrected on modern hardware thanks to Opus 5.5’s reverse-engineering capabilities; however, Anthropic, to the dismay of the community, has since restricted this. Many, I suspect, find it a little rich for the AI labs to lecture people on intellectual property rights, when they themselves trained their models on data with dubious provenance.
Of people’s concerns about data centres, power consumption is perhaps most salient. This is partly a worry about grid stability and energy prices, but also, due to the actions of developers, about climate change. Some data centres are side-stepping the question of grid connectivity by running gas turbines on-site, exacerbating not just climate change but local air pollution. If AI solves climate change, this is but a speed bump; however, this is likely not a view held by most people. Pew found in August 2026 that 54% of Americans believe AI will be mostly bad for the environment; this number is up from 39% in January of the same year.
At least everyone’s stock portfolios are up? Well, consider that only 62% of US households own any stocks in the first place, and then that most of the stock market is owned by the top 10%. In fact, many might see no upside in AI-driven stock market growth, but if the bubble were to pop, the resulting reverberations are a clear downside.
When these data centres are proposed, the democratic process is often subverted, or at least undermined. Local politicians bound by non-disclosure agreements face the community’s ire over shadowy developers and obscured end-clients. It’s a bad look with parallels to another high-salience issue of 2026: Flock cameras. This further fuels antagonism against data centres and AI.
Thus, for the median Western person, a data centre in their local community is a glaring, loud, visual reminder of AI. AI, which in the best case will free us from disease, labour, and suffering, but is more likely to further wealth inequality and rob them of their livelihood. AI, which according to its makers has a non-zero chance of killing us all. AI, which might increase their energy prices, hasten climate change, and pollute their air and water, while reducing their property value.
Neither the positive outcomes nor, obviously, the negative ones are seen as benefiting people. This at the cost of the climate, the democratic process, and a potential recession. Of course people hate data centres.

articles.title: Show HN: A terminal-native idle factory game, written in Rust with ratatui
articles.summary:
Hey HN readers!
I'm snipedbywifi (https://gitlab.com/snipedbywifi), and i've been working on terminactory. Please try it out if you'd like to play a cozy factory game while waiting for long agent tasks to finish!
The game is a factory game (overused niche, i know xD), but runs in your terminal. Reason i built it? glad you asked: So basically, it started off with me wanting a terminal-native factory game. Me and the modern 5.5 claude models made a base for the game that I liked, and then i went ham adding features / fixing some minor flaws (like adding claude code hooks so you recieve "telegrams" [the agent's responses], so you can review progress directly in-game). (yes, I had heavy AI assistance, disclaimer!!!)
Right now, the game has basic factory features you'd expect from a game like this (build stuff, delete stuff, measure how much you're earning, basic selection tools), along with a few more.. "unexpected" features. This includes a fake in-game browser that has a wiki, fake forums, some fun bits of lore, some more lore, a LOT more lore, and a research graph that shows how many items or how much RP (research points) you'd need to unlock something, and some more QOL features.
If anyone actually has this issue / want of a terminal-based game that runs alongside your agents so you don't doomscroll, do you have any suggestions, or additional ideas I could add?
It's hosted on GitLab, soo, that's one additional thing i'd like to mention
Thanks for reading!! snipedbywifi
(p.s. first HN post lol)
(p.s. p.s. there's a lot of hidden lore in the game, so.. lore-divers? you might like it?)
